column4: This is the section's clearest Quranic expansion: people are put into fire with the same s-l-y verb, their skins become cooked, replacement skins prolong the process, and they are made to taste punishment.

The section explicitly hears the cooking sense of 88:5 here: inahu is the food's time of readiness, while guests are told not to watch and wait for it; food, ripening time, and looking meet in one ayah.

Gold and silver are heated in Hellfire and then used to brand foreheads, sides, and backs; this enacts the section's dictionary image of metal made red-hot in fire and transfers that heat to the body.

Immediately after the command to affirm that truth is from the Lord and let people believe or disbelieve, the ayah gives the wrongdoers a drink like molten metal that roasts faces, joining denial, liquid, metal heat, and roasting.
Garments of fire are cut for the disputants and boiling water is poured over their heads, staging the section's fire and scalding drink as one treatment of the body.
The boiling water of 22:19 melts what is inside bellies as well as skins; this is a close bodily analogue to skins cooking in 4:56 and intestines being cut by hot water in 47:15.
Within a contrast between Paradise and Fire, boiling water is made to sever the drinkers' intestines; the drink is punishment rather than refreshment, as in the section's boiling spring.
The criminals circle between Hell and hamimin an, water whose heat has reached its endpoint; an carries exactly the terminal-heat sense developed for the spring in 88:5.
Naarun hamiyah repeats the exact phrase 'a fiercely hot fire' from 88:4.
The food of the sinner is compared with molten material boiling in bellies, turning an infernal meal into the cooking process developed by the section.
The substance boils like boiling water; this completes the kitchen sequence begun by the sinner's food in 44:43-45.
Those who have filled their bellies with zaqqum drink like desperately thirsty camels, the precise manner of drinking explicitly invoked by the section.

People plead the heat as a reason to stay behind, and the reply says Hell is far more intense in heat; the ayah turns ordinary hot weather, the same setting invoked by the section's h-m-y dictionary gloss, toward the section's fire.
The Flood begins when the tannur erupts or boils over; this literal oven scene activates the section's secondary image of a heated tannur, while also making a cooking vessel signal judgment.
The repeated Flood command begins when the tannur erupts or boils over, again making the oven named in the h-m-y gloss the threshold of judgment.
The command 'Enter/burn in it today' uses the s-l-y verb and gives persistent disbelief as the cause, explicitly joining the act in 88:4 to the kufr in 88:23.
The most wretched is said to enter the blazing fire with the same s-l-y verb used in 88:4.
This ayah identifies the person entering the fire in 92:15 as the one who denied and turned away, exactly the two acts brought together around 88:23.
The person who avoids the reminder enters the greatest fire with the same s-l-y verb; it directly parallels the section's fire and the surah's reminder.
Fire scorches their faces and leaves them grimacing, directly staging the face of 88:2-4 under fire's heat.
Their faces are turned over and over in the Fire while they regret disobedience; the turning evokes food exposed on every side to heat without inventing a separate implement.
The threatened punishment is a blazing fire, the fire into which the section's condemned face enters.
The blaze of 70:15 strips away the scalp or skin, adding another Quranic version of fire working directly on human covering.
The skin-stripping blaze calls the person who turned his back and went away; this is a close verbal and causal parallel to the one who turns away in 88:23.
God says He will make the rejecting speaker enter Saqar, using the same causative s-l-y form as the section's fire descriptions.
Saqar is described as scorching or altering human skin, making 74:26's entry into fire a bodily cooking scene like 4:56.
When people are thrown into Hell they hear it roar while it boils or surges, giving the fire itself the boiling action heard throughout the section's kitchen vocabulary.
They are dragged through boiling water and then made fuel in the Fire, directly sequencing the two punishments of 88:4-5.
They taste neither coolness nor drink there, denying the very relief that drinking normally supplies before 78:25 names the exception.
The only drink left after 78:24 is boiling water and foul fluid, a close counterpart to the boiling spring and the exclusive infernal food of 88:5-6.
Hell lies before the obstinate rejecter, who is given putrid fluid to drink; it is another punitive drink where water should relieve heat.
He gulps the drink but can scarcely swallow it, and death comes from every side without his dying; the ayah shows the bodily endurance of the drink in 14:16.
The ayah asks whether Paradise's hospitality is better than the zaqqum tree, explicitly presenting infernal food as a reversed meal.
Zaqqum is made a trial for wrongdoers, identifying the moral function of the meal introduced in 37:62.
The food tree grows from the very base of Hell, placing food production inside the fire itself.
Its fruit is pictured as repellent heads, continuing the concrete description of the food rather than merely naming punishment.
They eat from the tree and fill their bellies, making the condemned into diners at the Fire's meal.
After the food comes a mixture of boiling water, matching the section's immediate passage from fire to spring to food.
Their return is to Hell after this drink, enclosing the entire meal within fire.
The zaqqum tree introduces the infernal ingredient whose boiling is described in 44:45-46.
Zaqqum is called the food of the habitual sinner, giving the meal its eater before the next ayat describe it cooking inside him.
The sinner is seized and dragged into the middle of the blaze after the boiling-food image, making him part of the same cooking scene.
The punishment pours boiling water over his head, joining the internal boiling of 44:45-46 to external scalding.
The command to taste follows the boiling food and water, completing the same punitive culinary sequence as 4:56.
The people of the left are placed amid scorching wind and boiling water, combining heat and drink in a single setting.
Their shade is black smoke, an extension of the heated environment named in 56:42.
That shade is neither cool nor pleasant, explicitly withholding relief from the heat.
The infernal meal addresses the astray deniers, linking the menu that follows to the kufr component of the section.
The deniers eat from a zaqqum tree, a direct counterpart to the section's food in Fire.
They fill their bellies from it, emphasizing that the punishment operates as eating.
They drink boiling water on top of the food, repeating the section's food-and-hot-water pairing.
The whole meal is called their hospitality on the Day of Judgment, sharpening its character as a reversed banquet.
The order to make the great sinner enter the blaze uses the s-l-y root and treats the person as an object delivered into fire.

In the same infernal meal passage there is no hamim in the different sense of an intimate friend; the word's social sense stands beside the scalding hamim developed elsewhere and leads directly to 69:36's food.
There is no food except foul wound-wash, closely matching the exclusive 'no food except' construction of 88:6.
Only sinners eat that food, specifying the diners in the meal of 69:36.
Those who conceal revelation for a small price are said to consume nothing but fire in their bellies, collapsing wrongful eating and fiery punishment into one act.

After people exchange guidance for error and forgiveness for punishment, the ayah asks how they can endure the Fire; this closely matches the section's gloss of bearing fire's heat and severity and its self-made trap.
The Fire prepared for disbelievers has people and stones as fuel, making human bodies part of the furnace rather than merely its spectators.
The disbelievers themselves are called fuel for the Fire, an especially direct realization of the section's human-as-material cooking image.
Those who consume orphans' property are actually consuming fire into their bellies and will enter a blaze, joining eating, inner burning, and s-l-y in one ayah.
The commanded protection is from a Fire fueled by people and stones, again making persons the furnace's fuel.
The unjust are firewood for Hell, a concrete variant of people becoming the material that keeps the punishment burning.
The idolaters and what they worship are called fuel cast into Hell, turning both worshippers and objects into furnace charge.
The people of Fire are told to taste boiling water and foul fluid, explicitly combining punitive tasting with the section's hot drink.
This identifies the Hell denied by criminals before 55:44 says they circle between it and fully heated water; it supplies the denial side of that fire-and-water movement.
The most wretched avoids the reminder before entering the greatest fire in 87:12, paralleling the reminder in 88:21 and the turning-away response in 88:23.
Inside the greatest fire of 87:12, he neither dies nor lives; this specifies what it means to continue bearing its heat.
The warning of a blazing fire introduces the fire whose entrant and cause are specified in 92:15-16.
The person whose scales are light is the one for whom 101:11 names the same fiercely hot fire as 88:4.
His refuge is an abyss before 101:11 reveals it as the fiercely hot fire, adding the motion of falling into the heat.
They are shoved violently into Hellfire, a forceful counterpart to the section's entry into fire.
They are told that this is the Fire they used to deny, directly coupling the scene with denial.
The command to enter or burn in the Fire uses s-l-y and says endurance or lack of endurance makes no difference, echoing the gloss of suffering its heat and severity.
They are dragged on their faces into the Fire and told to taste Saqar's touch, joining face, fire, bodily contact, and taste.
Whenever they try to leave the anguish they are returned to the fire and ordered to taste the burning punishment, emphasizing repeated exposure like the replaced skins of 4:56.
Every attempted exit returns the defiantly disobedient to the Fire, where they are told to taste what they denied.
A person tries to shield himself from terrible punishment with his face and is told to taste what he earned, bringing the section's face and culinary verb together.
The command to taste the punishment of burning makes punishment both a fire and something consumed through taste.
Disbelievers are told to taste punishment and are assigned the punishment of Fire, joining kufr, tasting, and fire in one ayah.
The threatened punishment includes food that chokes, another infernal meal whose very ingestion becomes torment.
Disbelievers are said to eat as cattle eat, and in the same ayah the Fire is named as their lodging; ordinary feeding thus walks immediately into its own fiery end.
The people of Fire ask for water or provision from Paradise, but both are forbidden to disbelievers; thirst and food are present precisely through their punitive denial.
The greatest losers are those whose labor goes astray while they think they are doing well, a close nonlexical parallel to the exhausted worker moving toward his own trap.
Their works lose all weight because they denied the Lord's signs and meeting, supplying the kufr that makes the labor in 18:104 futile.
Hell is the payment for that denial and mockery, completing the movement from wasted labor in 18:104 to fire.
Those who intend a trap or plot are themselves the ones caught by a counterplot, a direct nonlexical equivalent of the bird entering the trap associated with the section's maslat.
The evil plot is said to close around none but its own makers, precisely expressing the section's image of laboring to set the trap one then enters.
Someone who acts in aggression and injustice is put into a fire with the causative s-l-y form; the ayah gives a concrete moral route into the section's fire.
The person who opposes the Messenger after guidance and follows another way is consigned to Hell with s-l-y; his chosen turning becomes the path into fire.
Those who lodge their people in the house of ruin enter Hell with the same s-l-y verb, extending the section's entry scene from an individual to misleaders and followers.
The person who chooses the immediate world is assigned Hell and enters it with s-l-y, blamed and banished; his desired shortcut becomes the trap leading to fire.
God knows best which groups most deserve siliyyan, burning in Hell; the verbal noun names the same exposure to fire as tasla.
The transgressors enter Hell with s-l-y, and the ayah calls it an evil resting place.
The deniers are tormented or burned over the Fire, picturing direct exposure to its surface and heat.
They are told to taste the burning they had demanded be hastened, completing 51:13's fire scene with culinary diction.
For the denying, astray person, the announced end is tasliyatu jahim, a burning or entry into Hell formed from the section's s-l-y root.
The wicked enter or burn in the blaze on Judgment Day with the same s-l-y root.
After arrogant rejection of the signs, they enter or burn in Hell with the s-l-y root, again joining denial to the section's verb.
The person given his record behind his back calls for destruction and enters a blaze with s-l-y.
Abu Lahab is promised entry into a flame-bearing fire with the same s-l-y verb.
Denial is visible in the disbelievers' faces as revelation is recited, and the ayah answers that hostile face with the Fire promised to them.
Those who burn or persecute believing men and women and do not repent receive both Hell and the punishment of burning, making inflicted fire return upon its agents.
Abraham promptly brings a roasted calf as hospitality; literal roasted meat and welcome form a sharp humane boundary against the section's person treated like meat in punitive fire.
Abraham's enemies command that he be burned in a fire, reproducing the scene of a person deliberately put into heat but with an unjust human agent.
God orders the same fire to become cool and safe for Abraham, showing that fire's heat is commanded and can be reversed rather than inherent or autonomous.
The people's plan is to kill or burn Abraham, but God saves him from the fire; the intended human roasting becomes a sign through rescue.
The opponents build a furnace or structure and plan to throw Abraham into its blaze, closely staging human placement into a prepared fire.
Their fiery plot ends with the plotters made low, an enacted reversal of the section's self-closing trap.
The people of the trench maintain a fuel-fed fire for believers, reversing the usual identity of the disbeliever who enters the section's fire.
The victims are attacked only for believing in God, fixing the moral reversal in the trench's fire scene before 85:10 turns burning back on the persecutors.
The people of Paradise are touched by no nasab, fatigue, a direct reversal of the weary condition named by nasibah in 88:3.
Paradise's residents say that no nasab or weariness touches them, explicitly setting blessed rest against the section's exhausted face.
For Solomon, God makes a spring of molten copper flow; the unusual meeting of spring and molten material resembles the section's superheated spring but functions as a gift and resource.
The righteous drink a cup mixed with camphor, a fragrant and cooling banquet image opposite the punitive hot drink.
That drink comes from a spring God's servants cause to flow abundantly, reversing the condemned person's encounter with the boiling spring.
The rewarded encounter neither scorching sun nor severe cold, defining a protected middle outside the section's extreme heat.
Their cup is mixed with ginger, another prepared drink whose flavor marks hospitality rather than torment.
A spring named Salsabil supplies that cup, a beneficent counterpart to the fully heated spring in 88:5.
A cup from a flowing spring is passed among Paradise's people, setting a hospitable spring-drink against the boiling mixture later in the same surah.
The drink is white and pleasurable, the sensory opposite of zaqqum and boiling water.
The drink causes neither harm nor loss of reason, whereas the section's liquid harms the drinker's body.

Those deceived by worldly play receive a drink of boiling water and painful punishment because they disbelieved; the specific drink-and-kufr combination matches the section even without its s-l-y verb.
Those who disbelieve are assigned boiling water to drink and painful punishment, again coupling the hot liquid to denial.
Blackened faces are told to taste punishment because they disbelieved after faith, bringing face, kufr, and punitive tasting together though no cooking verb appears.
Deniers confronted with the truth are told to taste punishment because of their disbelief; the culinary metaphor and kufr meet, but fire and hot water remain unstated here.
After corrupt worship at the House, they are told to taste punishment for disbelief; this supports the section's joining of kufr with tasting, although the ayah does not itself name heat.
Wrongdoers are told to taste the punishment of the Fire they denied, a direct fire-and-taste formulation.
When disbelievers are exposed to the Fire, they are told to taste punishment because they denied the meeting of that day.
The criminals wear pitch garments and fire covers their faces, combining a heat-ready substance with the face exposed to flame.
The rejected are gathered on their faces and lodged in Hell, whose blaze is increased whenever it subsides; the ayah joins face, fire, and renewed heating.
Those gathered on their faces toward Hell occupy the worst place and the most misguided path, making their movement itself lead face-first into the fire.
Those who bring an evil deed are cast face-first into the Fire and repaid only for what they did, a bodily version of walking into one's earned trap.
With collars and chains they are dragged toward the boiling water and fire named in 40:72; this ayah supplies the forced movement into the kitchen-like punishment.
Deniers are ordered to proceed toward what they used to deny, beginning a movement into the smoke and flame described in 77:30-31.
They proceed into a three-branched shadow of smoke, the atmospheric product of the fire named next.
The supposed shade is neither cooling nor protective against flame, specifically withholding relief from heat.
The punishment is God's kindled fire, emphasizing a fire deliberately brought to full burning heat.
That fire rises over the hearts, carrying the external flame inward as the section's food and drink do to bellies.
Job describes being touched by nusbin wa-adhab, weariness and torment; the pairing clarifies the same n-s-b exhaustion that stands beside punishment in 88:3-4.
The question 'Has the time not come?' uses the a-n-y root for a moment reaching due time; it moralizes the ripeness or arrival developed through food reaching readiness and water reaching full heat.
Hamiyyata al-jahiliyyah uses the h-m-y root for heated partisan zeal, while God sends tranquility; the human 'heat' is semantic rather than thermal but illuminates the root's extension.
Earlier peoples are seized with hardship so that they might tadarru, humble themselves; the d-r-a root differs from dari food but is placed in a punishment response that 6:43 says they refused.
When punishment came they failed to tadarru, humble themselves, because their hearts hardened; this other d-r-a sense helps explain humility arriving too late in the punished faces of the surah.
Every prophetic community is touched by adversity so that its people might tadarru, humble themselves; it supplies the root's penitential sense against the section's dari food.
Even when seized by punishment, they neither submit nor tadarru; the other d-r-a sense places failed humbling beside the road to final punishment.
Solomon's workers make massive fixed cauldrons; these Quranic pots provide a concrete counterpart to the section's dictionary picture of setting supports beneath a cooking pot.
The plotters devise a plot while God counters it without their awareness, a Quranic analogue to a hunter unaware that his trap will reverse.
Their plot ends in their own destruction, completing the self-trap movement begun in 27:50.
The opponents plot and God counters their plot; it supports the trap image through reversal, though it does not say that they literally enter their own device.
The disbelievers plot to confine, kill, or expel the Prophet while God counters their plotting, giving the section's trap a concrete human purpose and reversal.
The deniers are actively devising a scheme, corresponding to the labor of setting the section's trap.
God answers their scheme with His own, supplying the reversal that makes the trap unsafe for its makers.
In the same passage as the skin-stripping blaze, the sky becomes like molten material; this extends the molten-metal comparison used for the section's scalding water.
No hamim asks about another hamim on that day: here hamim means intimate friend rather than boiling water, and the alternate sense occurs only a few ayat before the blaze of 70:15.
The people of Hell lament that they have no hamim, intimate friend; this different sense of the word contrasts human warmth and aid with the punitive hamim drink.

They rush from graves as though racing toward a nusub, an erected goal or cult-stone; this may echo both the n-s-b act of setting a device and the section's movement into a trap, but the noun's precise image differs from a snare.
Their downcast eyes and enveloping humiliation complete 70:43's rush toward the erected goal; the relation to the section's weary, humbled face depends on that neighboring n-s-b echo.

The sworn 'filled' or 'kindled' sea may picture water made fiery, a striking analogue to the boiling spring; the participle al-masjur permits more than one reading, so the heat connection is uncertain.

At cosmic overturning the seas are sujjirat, which can mean kindled or made to overflow; on the kindling reading water and fire meet as in the section, but that lexical ambiguity keeps the link tentative.
Moses asks for the travelers' meal because the journey has brought them nasaban, fatigue; food and the same n-s-b weariness as 88:3 meet in one non-punitive ayah.
The false objects of worship can lure only one who is destined to be sali al-jahim, an entrant into Hell; the s-l-y root occurs at the end of a seduction that functions like the section's trap.
Whoever comes to the Lord as a criminal has Hell, where he neither dies nor lives; this directly repeats the endless endurance of heat made explicit beside 87:12.
For the disbelievers is Hellfire: death is not decreed for them and its punishment is not lightened, another exact account of continuing under the section's heat.

From the Fire they cry to be released so they can act differently, but their allotted lifetime and warning are recalled and they are told to taste; it completes 35:36 with failed escape and culinary diction.
The great sinner sent into the blaze did not believe in God, supplying the denial that causes the infernal meal of 69:35-37.
He did not urge feeding the poor, so the later denial of wholesome food and provision of foul food becomes a precise reversal of his failure to feed.
Earlier plotters build a scheme whose foundations God strikes, so its roof falls on them and punishment arrives unexpectedly; their own construction becomes the trap that closes on them.
The disbelievers cannot keep the Fire from their faces or backs and cannot be helped, placing the exposed face and body wholly inside the heat.
The disbelievers demand punishment be hastened while Hell already encompasses them, a self-incurred enclosure by fire.
Punishment covers them from above and below and they are told to taste what they used to do, adding culinary language to the enclosure named in 29:54.
Layers or canopies of fire lie both above and below them, making the punished body enclosed within heat like material inside an oven.
Pharaoh's people are exposed to the Fire morning and evening and then ordered into the severest punishment on the Hour, completing the reversal of their plot in 40:45.
The people of Fire repeatedly wish to leave it but cannot, and their punishment remains, another direct expression of having to endure its heat.
Successive communities enter the Fire and curse those before them, until all are gathered there; the ayah gives the social chain by which misleaders and followers enter the same furnace.
Each group is told it has a doubled share and to taste punishment for what it earned, adding the section's culinary verb to 7:38's fire.
The two gardens contain two flowing springs, a direct paradisal reversal of the fully heated water between which the criminals circle in 55:44.
A second pair of gardens has two gushing springs, repeating within the same surah the beneficent opposite of the boiling-water scene.
The Lord gives the rewarded a pure drink, directly opposing the impure, injurious liquids served to the condemned.
The righteous are given sealed pure wine to drink, presenting drink as protected reward rather than scalding punishment.
The rewarded drink is mixed with Tasnim, a prepared mixture that reverses the boiling mixture served after zaqqum.
Tasnim is a spring from which those brought near drink, an explicit beneficent counterpart to the section's boiling spring.
Maces of iron belong to the same scene as the poured boiling water of 22:19-20; the iron recalls the section's heated-metal gloss, though this ayah does not itself say the maces are hot.
God protects the believer from the evils of the plot, while an evil punishment closes around Pharaoh's people; this is another counter-trap immediately followed by their exposure to Fire.
Immediately after Abu Lahab is assigned a flaming fire, his wife is called a carrier of firewood; the neighbour extends the scene from one who burns to one who supplies fuel.
Those who forgot the meeting of their day are told to taste everlasting punishment for what they did; the taste metaphor and denial are specific, although this ayah does not name fire.

Among forbidden meats is what has been slaughtered upon nusub, erected cult-stones; it joins a different n-s-b form to meat preparation, whereas the section's dictionary usage sets supports beneath a pot.
On the approaching Day wrongdoers have no hamim in the sense of an intimate friend and no effective intercessor; the alternate social sense of the hot-water word appears within punishment context.
The punishment of Hell's criminals is not eased and they despair within it, specifying the unrelieved duration of the section's heat.
They call to Malik for their Lord to finish them, but are told they must remain; the wish for death completes 43:75's unrelieved punishment.
The threatened fire comes suddenly, stuns them, and cannot be repelled or delayed; it continues 21:39's face-and-back exposure, though its own wording leaves the fiery object implicit.
